title: ‘They don’t see us as humans’: Indigenous youth call for national day of action
content:

title: « Nous prenons soin les uns des autres. » : témoignages du square Cabot
content:
Au square Cabot de Montréal, où des Autochtones en situation d’itinérance se rassemblent depuis des décennies, la nouvelle selon laquelle un membre du Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM) avait été suspendu pour avoir uriné sur des personnes en situation d’itinérance a été accueillie avec peu de surprise.




Selon des habitués du secteur et des intervenants de rue œuvrant auprès des personnes en situation d’itinérance dans l’ouest du centre-ville, les rapports entre la police et les personnes itinérantes au square Cabot et dans les environs sont marqués par la méfiance et la peur.




Au cours d’une période de deux semaines, les personnes interrogées par APTN Nouvelles au square Cabot ont affirmé avoir reçu de nombreuses contraventions, représentant des centaines de dollars d’amende, pour non-paiement du titre de transport ou pour avoir traversé la rue Sainte-Catherine hors des intersections autorisées. Des personnes buvant de l’alcool dans le square ont aussi rapporté avoir reçu des amendes pour possession de contenants ouverts. Bien peu cherchent à payer leurs contraventions. Pour eux, en recevoir une nouvelle fait tout simplement partie de la réalité au square Cabot, bien que cela puisse éventuellement fournir à la police un prétexte pour les arrêter.

title: Yukon court dismisses wrongful death lawsuit against Whitehorse shelter operator
content:
The Supreme Court of Yukon has dismissed a wrongful death lawsuit against the operator of the Whitehorse emergency shelter.

Chief Justice Suzanne Duncan said in a Nov. 6 decision that the lawsuit was brought after the one-year limitation period under the Yukon’s Fatal Accidents Act.

Josephine Hager, 38, a Selkirk First Nation citizen, died at the shelter on Feb. 1, 2023. Her father, Dale Joe, filed the lawsuit last October.

An inquest in April 2024 heard that Hager, who lived in a supportive housing unit at the shelter, died from a lethal mix of morphine and alcohol.

The lawsuit claims Connective, the non-profit organization operating the shelter, and five unnamed staff members were negligent in Hager’s death.

However, Connective argued in an application that Joe, who filed the suit more than two years after his daughter’s death, missed the one-year deadline under the act.

According to the decision, Joe said he wasn’t aware of the circumstances surrounding his daughter’s death and its potential wrongful nature until shortly after the 2024 inquest, more than a year after she died.

The decision also notes that his mother and brother died within a year of each other, adding to his grief.

author: Fraser Needham
title: Outgoing Green Party leader says Carney is the most ‘opaque, unaccountable person in politics’
content:
Elizabeth May says Prime Minister Mark Carney is perhaps the most challenging party leader she has had to work with in more than four decades in politics.




“Accountability is really important and Mr. Carney is the most opaque, unaccountable person in politics I think I have ever seen,” the Green Party MP said.




May stepped down as Green Party leader earlier this month, making way for former Kitchener, Ontario MP Mike Morrice to take over the party’s reins.




She will continue on as the MP for the riding of Saanich-Gulf Islands in British Columbia.




One of the reasons May voted in favour of the 2025 budget was Carney’s pledge to respect Canada’s Paris commitments on climate change.




With the Liberal government’s continued backing of oil and gas projects, it is now highly unlikely Canada will meet these commitments.




Carney, a former governor of both the Bank of Canada and Bank of England, has often been touted as the right leader at the right time due to the country’s ongoing trade issues with the Trump administration in the U.S.

author: Emma Honeybun
title: Majority of reported ‘serious’ injuries to Indigenous children in Manitoba tied to sexual assault
content:
Warning: this story discusses child abuse and suicide




Manitoba’s youth advocate says more than half of serious injury reports involving kids are linked to sexual assault, and that 71 per cent of victims are Indigenous children.




“It’s pretty telling,” said Sherry Gott, the executive director of 

Manitoba Advocate for Children and Youth (MACY)

. “The numbers are pretty high, 53 per cent of our reports are a result of sexual assault or sexual exploitation, and the majority of those are Indigenous children.”




MACY is a non-partisan advocacy organization funded by the provincial government.




Alongside investigative work, it provides advocacy and social services to youth and families, which can result in safety plans, placements and post-release mental health and addictions support for children and young adults (aged 18 to 20).




Since 2000, her office has published annual reports which summarize trends, data and updates with respect to youth in Manitoba, as well as the organization’s recommendations to the province.




In 2023, the organization created its Serious Injuries Reviews and Investigations program, in response to a recommendation from the provincial 

Phoenix Sinclair Inquiry

, created to examine the circumstances surrounding the neglect, physical abuse and 

eventual murder

 of the five-year-old girl in Fisher River Cree Nation almost a decade prior.

title: Gitxsan Huwilp Government in B.C. wants train hauling stopped in territory after latest derailment
content:

Gitxsan Huwilp Government

The First Nation said in a statement that the latest derailment has reignited its call for the “immediate stop to all train hauling” in its traditional territories and fishing waterways, calling the practice dangerous.




Several railcars jumped the tracks on Tuesday, spilling diesel and sending some cars loaded with forest products into the Skeena River about 15 kilometres west of Terrace.




CN Rail announced the track had been repaired and train traffic resumed on Thursday, while the two crew members who were injured in the derailment have been released from hospital.




The company said environmental protection measures are in place in the river and specialized environmental response teams remain at the site, working to contain and recover spilled diesel fuel and removing derailed equipment.




The First Nation said it is the second such incident in eight months, after a mudslide derailed grain cars travelling along the river south of Prince Rupert in March, resulting in a spill of nearly 8,000 litres of diesel.




Hereditary Chief Toby Howard said the latest accident demonstrates the continuing risks posed by freight transportation through Gitxsan territory.

author: Jesse Staniforth
title: Nunavut child advocate considered suing territorial government over child welfare stonewalling
content:
Nunavut’s child advocate says she was ready to take the territory’s Department of Family Services to court because of what she characterized as the DFS stonewalling her office’s access to information pertaining to Nunavummiut children in care. 




Jane Bates told Nunavut’s legislative assembly in September that despite an information-sharing protocol, the department was deciding for itself whether, and when, her office should be involved in assessing its conduct.




“This situation has become so serious,” the Representative for Children and Youth (RCYO) told legislators, “that earlier this year I advised the deputy minister that, unless the underlying issue concerning the RCYO’s statutory authority and the department’s corresponding obligations could be resolved, I was prepared to withdraw from the GN–RCYO Protocol and seek the assistance of the Nunavut Court of Justice to ensure that our office could carry out its statutory mandate.







“If significant limits, safeguards and independent oversight are not put in place, the department will continue to operate in the same manner with the same results.”




These details are from notes shared with APTN News of Bates’s presentation on the crisis in Nunavut’s child-welfare system delivered on Sept. 24 and 25 to the territory’s Legislative Assembly’s Standing Committee on Oversight of Government Operations and Public Accounts.

title: Canada commits $6.2M to 2028 North American Indigenous Games
content:
The federal government is increasing its investment in the 2028 North American Indigenous Games by $1.3 million, bringing its total contribution to $6.2 million. 




According to the government, the money is intended to expand Indigenous participation in sport and strengthen opportunities for First Nations, Inuit and Métis athletes across the country.




Secretary of State for Sport Adam van Koeverden announced the funding Thursday during the official launch of the 2028 Games, which will bring an estimated 5,250 participants representing as many as 700 Indigenous nations to Winnipeg and communities across Manitoba from July 9 to 23, 2028.




The federal government says the host province is expected to match its $6.2-million investment in the 2028 Games. 




The investments come as the federal government faces the broader challenge of addressing barriers to sport participation in Indigenous communities, where access to culturally relevant programming, facilities, coaching and competitive opportunities remains central to developing sustainable pathways for Indigenous athletes.




Van Koeverden said the investments are intended to advance reconciliation while creating opportunities for Indigenous youth to participate, compete and pursue athletic excellence.

author: The Canadian Press
title: Top court won’t hear bid for class-action lawsuit on behalf of Indigenous children
content:
The Supreme of Court of Canada will not hear a bid to certify a class-action lawsuit against Ottawa on behalf of Indigenous children who were taken from their families while living away from reserves and placed in non-Indigenous care.




The class-action claim is based on Canada’s duty to protect Indigenous children in care from harm, specifically as it relates to the loss of their identity.




The lawsuit challenges Canada’s role between Jan. 1, 1992 and Dec. 31, 2019 in allowing Indigenous children in state care to be placed in non-Indigenous homes.




In 2022, the Federal Court ruled the matter could go ahead as a class action for those affected in all provinces and territories.




Last year, the Federal Court of Appeal overturned that decision, saying Canada does not have possession, power or control over documents and information relevant to the claim.




The Court of Appeal also said the preferable course would be proceedings before courts that can compel the participation of provinces responsible for administration and delivery of child and family services to off-reserve Indigenous children.

title: First Nations are passing laws to protect their communities, but who will enforce them?
content:
First Nations leaders and legal experts are pressing the federal government to address a longstanding gap in Canada’s justice system. They say while First Nations have the authority to make their own laws, enforcing and prosecuting violations of those laws remains a significant challenge.




The issue took centre stage Tuesday at the 2026 

National Conference on the Future of Enforcement of First Nations Laws

 in Gatineau, Que., where discussions focused on the responsibilities of federal and provincial governments, including the RCMP, to recognize and enforce First Nations laws.




At the centre of the discussions are two pieces of federal legislation sponsored by Sen. Mary Jane McCallum. Bill S-223 is proposing amendments to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act, and Bill S-224, which is proposing amendments to the Director of Public Prosecutions Act.




For Chief Robert Louie of Westbank First Nation, who moderated Tuesday’s conference discussions, the proposed legislation represents a straightforward but significant step toward recognizing First Nations jurisdiction.




“These are very straightforward things and the federal government can easily do that very simply,” Louie said.




He said the proposed amendments would clarify the RCMP’s responsibilities in enforcing First Nations laws while establishing mechanisms to ensure those laws can be prosecuted.

author: Charlotte Morritt-Jacobs
title: While addiction treatment ends, recovery doesn’t, so N.W.T. residents want continuation of care
content:
Maria Hajcik spent roughly 20 years struggling with her addiction in Yellowknife. When she returned home after receiving treatment in Calgary, she had nowhere to go.




“I couldn’t go to my mom’s house and I couldn’t go somewhere that I knew because I was so vulnerable and so scared,” Hajcik said. “I was frightened that I’d get back into the same old things.”




Hajcik has now been clean and sober for 13 years. She is the community and wellness supervisor at the Tree of Peace Friendship Centre in Yellowknife, where she supports people dealing with active addiction and those in recovery.




Her lived experience shapes how she approaches the work. For Hajcik, getting someone into a treatment facility is only one part of recovery. What happens when they return home is equally important.




“If there’s no aftercare, there’s nothing,” Hajcik said. “If people go to treatment and they come back and there’s nothing to do afterwards, they’ll get back into the same old routine, the same old people, the same old lifestyle that they know.”

title: Chief in Yukon raises alarm over looming Parks Canada job cuts
content:
The chief of a First Nation in Yukon is raising concerns about potential staffing cuts at Parks Canada and how they could impact the First Nation’s co-management agreement with the federal agency.




“We are concerned about it, but we don’t know what the implications of this are because we haven’t had that kind of discussion yet,” said Kluane First Nation Chief Bob Dickson.




The First Nation co-manages 

Kluane National Park and Reserve

 — one of three national parks in the territory — along with Parks Canada and the Champagne and Aishihik First Nations as part of its final agreement.




Dickson said he learned of the cuts one day before letters were sent to almost 3,000 Parks Canada staff across the country.




The cuts come amid federal belt-tightening, with plans to scrap the equivalent of 500 full-time jobs at the agency to save $145 million in spending over the next three years.




In the North, potential job cuts could sting especially hard.




In Yukon, 58 of 137 Parks Canada jobs are affected — about 42 per cent of its total workforce in the territory, according to the agency.




Dickson said it’s not yet clear how staffing cuts would impact the park’s co-management agreement and employment opportunities for the handful of Kluane citizens who mainly work there seasonally.

title: Mohawk teacher, 73, earns McGill’s first PhD in Indigenous Language Revitalization
content:
By her own estimate, Mary Onwá:ri Tekahawákhwen McDonald has taught the Mohawk language to thousands of students over the past decades, from elementary school all the way to university level.




But when someone suggested she might pursue a PhD, the idea of returning to class in her 70s was a daunting prospect.




“(I said) ‘no, why would I want to do that?'” the now-73-year-old says with a laugh. ” … How do I compete with 20-year-olds? Can I really do this?”




Today, the Mohawk educator, linguist and elder can add the title of “doctor” to her list of accomplishments. Earlier this year, she became the first person to graduate from McGill University with a PhD in Indigenous Language Revitalization.




McDonald said she was eventually convinced to apply to the program out of a desire to write down the knowledge she’s accumulated over 45 years of teaching and studying language.




McDonald, who is from the Akwesasne community that straddles Quebec, Ontario and New York, is a native Mohawk speaker who only learned to speak English in second grade.




She went on to study Iroquoian linguistics, with a concentration in Mohawk, in university in Albany, N.Y., and later got a teaching certification in Ontario.

title: InFocus: Is adopting permanent daylight saving time a mistake?
content:
Many of us know how we feel when it’s time to change our clocks back in the fall and forward in the spring. Sleepy – maybe even a little disoriented.

Well, on Nov. 1, citizens in six provinces and territories didn’t experience any of that because their governments scrapped the dreaded seasonal time change.

Governments had two choices: stick with standard time or daylight saving time. Standard time gives you more sun in the morning – while daylight time gives you extended sun in the evening.

Most chose to extend daylight into the evening.

But will they regret their decision?

This week on InFocus, David Prerau, one of the world’s foremost experts on daylight saving time, explains why they might.

“What happened in the U.S. anyway is nobody was much against it until it actually occurred in January 1974,” Prerau, the author of Seize the Daylight, told host Cierra Bettens. “We had an incident in 1974 where there was an energy crisis, an unexpected energy crisis. author: Emma Honeybun
title: Manitoba group needs $17M to bring 3,000 Indigenous artefacts home
content:
A Manitoba-based organization is trying to raise $17 million to bring 3,000 Indigenous artefacts home from Switzerland.

“It doesn’t matter what tribe you’re from, it’s important that our people come together to bring these home to our Nations,” said Karl Stone, spiritual advisor of the group Return the Sacred. “And have these stored in a place where they can be kept for our own medicine people, within our own communities.

Return the Sacred, formerly called the Bringing Them Home Project, is a grassroots organization formed in 2025.

“That’s the way these sacred bundles should be taken care of, I believe. And these sacred bundles should be taught to the next generation.”

The group, headed by executive director Coleen Rajotte, returned from a week-long trip to Switzerland Thursday and held a news conference in Winnipeg.

Since June 2025, the group has been in communication with a private collector, Vincent Escriba, who ran the Indian Land Museum in Gossau, Switzerland.

The museum contained over 5,000 artefacts from North and South America, as well as several countries in Africa. They’re all part of Escriba’s private collection, which he has been growing for the majority of his adult life.

“He is actually a kind, gentle person,” Rajotte said. “He became enamoured with Indigenous people and Indigenous culture.”

She said he “spent his entire life travelling to North America,” 50 trips overall, collecting the items and purchasing other private collections in full.

“That’s how he’s collected such a vast quality,” she said. “We do believe him that he wants to work with us,” she said. “He’s now 70 years old, he’s put all his energy and all his money into this collection, and now he wants to sell it back.”

The Indian Land Museum closed in December 2025, when Escriba decided to retire. Since then, the artefacts have been stored in boxes in a private warehouse, awaiting sale.

Prior to its closure, the chief of Pikangikum First Nation, a community located in northern Ontario, had been advised of the collection’s fate. The chief told Gerald Neufeld, a long-time researcher based in Winnipeg, who created the group in an effort to bring the artefacts home.

The collection includes headdresses, unopened medicine bags, medicine and corn husk masks, pipes, totem poles, canoes, and several other types of artefacts that carry spiritual and cultural weight, Rajotte said.

Escriba also owns several boxes of textbooks, both in English and German.

Over several days, the group met with Escriba and took hundreds of photos of descriptions, contained in stacks of binders, which identified each object, along with its origin, in German.

They have not been able to confirm when all of the artefacts were made, but estimate most left Canada between 1840 and 1860.

Similarly, Rajotte said she is still working to figure out what came from where, but has so far been able to confirm several objects were from Nations in southern Alberta and North Dakota.

They also negotiated with Escriba and determined how much it would cost to purchase the items and return them to North America: $14.5 million, as well as an additional $3 million to cover transportation and handling of the items.

“Of course, there’s lots of opinions,” Rajotte said about Escriba’s decision to sell, rather than donate, the items back to the Nations they originally came from.

In California, she continued, the California Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act requires that all state-funded agencies, museums and universities must return any Indigenous cultural items, without a cost, by law.

However, even if the same laws existed in Canada, the situation with Escriba would be different, Rajotte said, due to his collection being private.

She said they are planning to negotiate with Escriba about lowering the price, or a long-term payment plan, but she doesn’t believe he’ll budge when it comes to the bill.

However, he has extended the sale’s deadline, which was originally set for payment by the end of December 2026.

Rajotte said she predicts it will take “at least” a year to appraise, document and pay for the entire collection.

So far, Heritage Canada has covered the initial trip to Switzerland, but there have been no additional conversations with public or private funders regarding the price of the collection itself.

“Our peoples’ sacred belongings that are in museums all over the world should be returned to the original people of this true land,” Stone said. “The bundles need to be protected … need to be cared for in a sacred way.”

Rajotte said, additionally, items are seen as living relatives, “ and the fact that they’re in a warehouse right now … no one’s spending time with them, visiting with them, makes me very very sad.”

She said her “biggest fear” was running out of time and not being able to purchase the collection, and that it will then be sold to private buyers and live out the rest of their days in office buildings in Dubai or New York City.

Stone said “it’s out of [his] hands,” but that he prays “that the right thing is done.

“It’s up to him [Escriba], but in our culture, we don’t believe there’s a price tag on anything that is sacred,” he said. “It’s sacred to us, that’s our way of life, that’s our culture, our belief, and hopefully something good will come of this.”

Return the Sacred will be hosting a fundraiser on Dec. 3. Money from the first event will go towards creating a digital archive and hiring a larger team.

The group’s short-term plan will be to translate each artefact description from German to English, with the use of artificial intelligence and a translator to double-check, to determine which artefact belongs to who.

Rajotte is encouraging “anyone with deep pockets” to reach out to the organization and donate to the cause.

“We’re working really hard to make sure we get all these items back to Turtle Island where they belong,” she said.

author: Leanne Sanders
title: First Nations Leadership Council sends open letter to the prime minister, Indigenous Services over delay in passing Bill S-2
content:
In an open letter to Prime Minister Mark Carney and Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull Masty, the First Nations Leadership Council (FNLC) is calling for an immediate end to the second-generation cut-off.

The FNLC is made up of the B.C. Assembly of First Nations, First Nations Summit and the Union of B.C. Indian Chiefs. It’s calling for an end to sex and race-based discrimination in the Indian Act, and removal of the second-generation cutoff.

“We fully support the amendments to Bill S-2 made by the Standing Senate Committee on Indigenous Peoples and adopted by the Senate of Canada on December 4, 2025,” the FNLC said in the letter.

“Further, we are concerned with the Minister of Indigenous Services Canada’s (ISC) use of a secretive process regarding the new standalone legislation, which violates the legal duty to consult in good faith.”

The second-generation cutoff is when a person, under section 6(1) of the Indian Act, passes status to a child no matter who the other parent is. But a person under section 6(2) can pass it on only if the other parent is also registered as “status” under the Indian Act.

After two generations of parenting with someone who is not registered, the third generation is out. That is the second-generation cut-off.

The FNLC maintains that the immediate elimination of the second-generation cut-off is supported by UN human rights bodies including the UN Human Rights Committee, the UN Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination Against Women, and, in May 2026, the UN Expert Mechanism on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples.

“For months, Bill S-2 has been stalled in the Standing Committee on Indigenous and Northern Affairs (INAN Committee), while the Minister insisted upon further consultations and then argued for broader registration reform and confused the issues of band membership and self-determination over citizenship with Indian status, and is now proposing new draft legislation. These deceptive tactics are a red herring to distract and delay the passage of Bill S-2,” the letter stated.

First Nations Summit Political executive Robert Phillips said in an interview with APTN News that it’s frustrating that “we’ve governed ourselves for thousands of years. And to remove second-generation cutoff and maybe replace it with universal one parent rule, or introducing legislation-and then it’s stalling?”

“We’re getting to the point where now we’re in argumentative stage…I do believe we need to be at a table and say that the authority should rest with First Nations and those that have treaties or those that have Aboriginal rights like here in British Columbia…,” Phillips said.

According to Phillips, Gull-Masty has invited “select First Nations leaders” to consult with ISC on new draft legislation to address the second-generation cut-off.

In the letter to Carney and Gull-Masty, the FNLC said, “we understand that… the minister has invited select First Nations leaders to consult with ISC regarding new draft legislation to address the second-generation cut-off, on the condition that they sign a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA), which binds them to not disclose any information that is shared with them for a period of five years, unless that information is disclosed to the public by the Minister.”

That doesn’t sit well with the FNLC.

“Using NDAs to convene meetings with selected leaders blocks First Nations leaders from consulting their Nations, members, technical and legal advisors. This secretive and selective process is an alarming escalation of the government’s tactics to undermine the broad support of First Nations.”

Senators vote to end the second-generation cutoff for ‘status Indians’

According to a statement from Gull-Masty’s office, a “collaborative process” on the second-generation cut off and section 10 voting thresholds concluded at the end of July, where the government invited First Nations to “put forward their own proposals and solutions to address these inequities in the Indian Act.

“We heard a range of perspectives, proposals, and priorities, alongside a shared sense of urgency: the second generation cut-off must be addressed,” according to a statement provided by Gull-Masty’s office. “While the Collaborative Process has now concluded, the work continues. We are currently reviewing the proposals, feedback and perspectives shared through the process to inform next steps, including legislative reform.”

The FNLC said the process goes against “the vast majority of First Nations across Canada” and introducing new standalone legislation ignores “broad support from First Nations and First Nations rights-holders…and directly contravenes the mandate of the vast majority of First Nations across Canada, who are on record supporting the immediate passage of Bill S-2 as amended by the Senate.”

title: ISC minister says she was not expecting Kinew’s comments about abolishing the Indian Act
content:

“I think that’s the initiative I was hoping to see as a minister coming out of that space because you have to increase the responsibility, the partnership, the role of the provincial government in the path beyond the Indian Act.”

author: Bruce De La Cruz
title: ‘Where is the accountability?’: Nunavut’s child advocate says territory’s protection issues aren’t being addressed
content:
Another scathing report from the federal auditor general looking into Nunavut’s child protection system came as no surprise to Jane Bates, the territory’s child welfare advocate.

On Nov. 3, deputy auditor general Andrew Hayes released the latest in a series of damning reports outlining how Nunavut is failing to protect Inuit children in care of the state.

For Bates, who has already written extensively about the issue, it came as no surprise.

“These concerns have been reported on, recommendations have been made about them, and yet they remain unaddressed to the detriment of children, youth, and families,” Bates told APTN News, “which is really the fundamental issue that everyone should be really concerned about, is the lack of follow through.

“We’re not talking about buildings. We’re not talking about bicycles. We’re talking about children and youth and their families. And so it’s deeply concerning.”

Hayes’ report outlined found that “fundamental weaknesses” in Nunavut’s child welfare system and its handling of the territory’s most vulnerable “remain unresolved” in audits going back to 2011.

“When children are removed from their homes and are placed in foster care for protection, the department takes on responsibility for their safety and well being,” Hayes said at a news conference on Nov. 3. “Yet it could not consistently demonstrate that basic safeguards, intended to protect children and place them in safe environments, were being followed.”

According to the latest report, approximately 400 children and youth are in Nunavut’s foster care system; the majority are Inuit.

Hayes said his office reviewed 40 cases and found issues that go back more than a decade.

The major concerns included that Nunavut’s Department of Family Services didn’t maintain required monthly in-person contact in more than 90 per cent of the cases; only performed 52 per cent of required evaluations for home safety” and, in 75 per cent of the cases, failed to give important information about a child to caregivers.

“Where is the accountability here? And again, we’re hearing, ‘oh, yes, we accept all the recommendations and we’re going to make changes.’ Where have you been? This has been upwards of 15 years. And we shouldn’t still be having this conversation.”

One Inuk family services employee who spoke to APTN News on condition that we grant anonymity, said the lack of Inuit staffing is the biggest concern.

“There’s like 30 per cent Inuit employed by this department,” the employee said. “I think if we had an Inuk supervisor, it would make a difference. Someone who knows the culture.”

Clayton Greaves, assistant deputy minister of Family Services Wellness Division, oversees the operations for the child welfare system in Nunavut.

“When I reviewed the report, and I hear what’s happening, we accept the other general recommendations and we accept that there’s work that’s in front of us that we have to do,” he said.

Greaves emphasized the challenges in running the child welfare system and said they’re doing the best with what they have.

“When we look at the report, we have to be careful that we don’t draw the conclusion that the gaps that we see is directly related to children being harmed,” he said. “And I wanted to make sure that we’re able to emphasize that. Yes, there are challenges with our new information system. We recognize and accept, you know, the recommendation, like I said, from what the Auditor General reported.”

Auditor general funds Nunavut foster care continues to fail vulnerable children

According to Bates’ own report that was filed in September, harm is coming to children.

“In the Reviews of Critical Injuries and Deaths program, reports of sexualized violence increased significantly, from eight in 2024–2025 to 22 in 2025–2026, while the number of young people who died by suicide tragically increased to 13,” she wrote in a report tabled in the Nunavut legislature.

“Children and youth who grow up in care, there’s been numerous studies done on the trajectory for young people,” she told APTN. “The outcomes are not good for children who grow up in care. They’re away from their families. They’re away from their culture. They lose their language.

“Children have the right to grow up with their families. They have a right to be protected. These are their fundamental rights under the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child. And currently, in Nunavut, that is not happening.”

title: Grieving mother livestreams private Manitoba police watchdog meeting to force transparency
content:
A grieving mother is taking transparency into her own hands by livestreaming meetings with Manitoba’s police watchdog and justice minister over the lack of independent investigation into her daughter’s violent arrest and subsequent death.




Crystal Delvenne said she chose to livestream the meetings to Facebook because she’s “lost trust in these systems” over the last few months following the Independent Investigation Unit of Manitoba’s (IIU) refusal to investigate an arrest by the Brandon Police Service (BPS).




Crystal’s daughter Cassity told her police beat her during the June 12 arrest, leaving her with bruised ribs, bleeding ears and hearing loss.




Cassity was found dead in her apartment of an unknown cause nine days later. Police said Cassity’s death is unrelated to her arrest.




On Friday, BPS announced it concluded its investigation into her death, saying a “definitive cause of death has been determined,” but added it could not share it publicly due to privacy laws and out of respect for the family.




According to the family, nothing has been received at the time this story was published.

author: Tamara Pimentel
title: On the Outside: Is Manitoba contributing to its own crime problem?
content:
Otessa Lanceley waits at the Unicity bus stop in Winnipeg. It’s the first stop as you enter the city from the west.




This is where she is dropped off every time she gets released from the Women’s Correctional Centre in the nearby town of Headingley.




“I’ve been doing this my whole life,” she said, as she waits for the bus that will take her straight downtown.




“I’ve been in and out of jail every year since I was 12.”




Being left on the outskirts of the city, without a plan and with nothing more than a bus ticket and the clothes they were arrested in, is a common story for people exiting Manitoba’s provincial correctional system.




“There’s hardly no resources for somebody to grasp on to,” Lanceley said to APTN Investigates, “Especially if they’re only there for a little bit, they get dropped right back off to where they started.”

author: Emma Honeybun
title: Prime minister announces $1B for housing, new hospital to ‘tackle’ homelessness in Winnipeg
content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney joined Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew and the mayor of Winnipeg to announce a joint funding venture to build more than 2,000 new homes and an addictions treatment centre in the middle province’s capital.

The federal government will be allocating $1 billion overall, with $800 million going to the homes and the remaining $200 million going to the proposed Winnipeg Mental Health and Addictions Centre, as well as the refurbishment of similar facilities.

“There’s no simple answer,” Carney said. “This is a hard problem. And hard problems demand the humility to learn from previous well-intentioned efforts that have fallen short.”

Funds will also go to supporting local, grassroots organizations that are already involved in addressing the homelessness crisis, including End Homelessness Winnipeg, the North End Women’s Centre, and Chalmers Neighbourhood Renewal Corporation.

Carney said the partnership is one project in an “unprecedented” $30 billion allocation in the 2026 budget, with the end goal of ending homelessness in Canada in 10 years.

“Help works,” he said, which extends to housing and healthcare.

Alongside federal, provincial and municipal governments, funding for these Winnipeg-based projects will also be provided by First Nation governments such as the Southern Chiefs’ Organization (SCO), as well as private funders such as True North Sports and Entertainment, owner of the Winnipeg Jets and the primary investor in several major infrastructure projects downtown.

“It’s the first time in our country’s history where every level of government has come together to tackle homelessness,” Kinew said. “Including First Nations and Métis governments.”

“The reality is that a huge part of what we see is that [in the past] failed policies like residential schools left a disproportionate number of Indigenous people vulnerable to the ravages of addictions. And the only way for us to find a solution is to have the full participation and engagement of the leaders of those people.”

He said, “A challenge for Indigenous Peoples in Canada has never been that Indigenous Peoples don’t know the solutions. Absolutely we do. The challenge has been that we didn’t have access to the resources and to the decision-making tables to make that happen.”

Carney said that previous government and community efforts to address homelessness have been “inadequately resourced, poorly co-ordinated, and not sustained.”

He said it’s “imperative” that this new strategy succeeds.”

“In Canada, we know we’re not perfect, but we always strive to be good,” Carney said. “We do things because they’re right, not because they’re easy. Ending homelessness is hard; it’s good, and it’s right. And it will require more than compassion.

“It will require ambition, execution, and partnership amongst all levels of government with contributions from philanthropy and business,” Carney added.

There was no determined answer when it came to where most of the 2,000 planned units will be built, but the first 373 are currently being developed inside of Wehwehneh Bahgahkinahgohn, formerly known as the Hudson’s Bay Building, just down the street from the Manitoba Legislature.

The building was acquired by the SCO in 2022, and is scheduled to be complete in 2028. Funding is supported through a partnership with True North.

Jamil Mahmood, the executive director of Main Street Project, a major non-profit addictions treatment centre and homeless shelter, said that additional housing would be useful anywhere in the downtown core.

The organization’s emergency shelter on Main Street has been affected by several fires in 2026, beginning in January. The most recent was on Oct. 31.

Money from this announcement will help refurbish the building, which housed over 2,900 people in 2025, according to its annual report.

“We know that’s where people are, we know that’s where the resources are, so the more you can put housing up where resources are is great,” he said.

“I think over time we can definitely expand that … from the core area to different areas, but then you also need to move resources to those places,” he added. “So we believe a decentralized model would work over time, but right now we have resources downtown.”

Mahmood said “the big thing,” however, is the inclusion of wrap-around support on-site, and staff who can remain there to help.

“I think that helps a lot of people really feel more comfortable with this housing,” he said. “And also, the reverse option is people stay in encampments or they stay on street corners.”

End Homelessness Winnipeg, a non-profit that, through its data collection, determined that every one in four homeless people in Winnipeg is Indigenous, stated the announcement was a “significant opportunity for Winnipeg,” after the fact.

“We have an opportunity to move beyond managing homelessness and toward ending it,” CEO Jennifer Moore Rattray said in the statement. “Housing is medicine, but housing alone is not enough. We need prevention, mental wellness services and sustained community supports.”

Similar to Mahmood’s point, Moore Rattray also noted that “the solutions are already in our communities, led by people and organizations who know what works.

“This once-in-a-lifetime investment could give us the resources to bring those solutions to scale and create lasting change for the people we serve.”

The additional money going towards mental health care would be to help address the issues which may render someone homeless at their source, Carney said.

Now not everyone without a home needs health care, but most desperately do,” he said. “Nine in 10 people on the Winnipeg streets face a health challenge, most often addiction, mental illness or both. And for them, the emergency room becomes their only respite, but it’s a temporary respite. They’re treated, discharged, and then they go straight back onto the street. and the cycle begins again.”

As of Friday afternoon, the wait time at St. Boniface Hospital’s emergency room was 15 hours long, according to the Winnipeg Regional Health Authority.

He said having improved mental health care would decrease the number of people visiting emergency rooms as a last resort.

In Toronto, Carney added, emergency room visits went down 80 per cent because of the Fred Victor Dunn House, a four-storey apartment building with on-site social support for people who were previously homeless or struggling with addiction. A new mental health centre in Winnipeg would fill the same need.

Kinew described the centre as “a new health care campus” and said that Manitoba has needed to “do more” when it comes to mental health and addictions support, and not only for the homeless population.

“I want to be clear,” he added, “yes, there’s a lot of people we drive by on the street doing the fentanyl fold, but there’s people in the suburbs in a basement who are struggling right now, there’s people in rural communities who are struggling from the very same vices and very same disease, and this service is going to be there for everybody in Manitoba who wants recovery.”

Mark Chipman, the executive chairman of True North, had originally proposed the idea of a new hospital, according to Kinew.

Alongside Wehwehneh Bahgahkinahgohn, True North is also responsible for the $650 million redevelopment of Portage Place Shopping Mall, soon-to-be the site of a mixed-use True North Campus, which will include housing, health care centre, grocery store, and urban greenspaces.

Chipman said the number of people “with an acquired brain injury” due to toxic drugs “is staggering,” and the new centre will serve as “an entry point to stabilise them, and then find the correct supports for them.

“Every person’s got a different story, and then those supports are co-located and lined up,” he said.

Speaking at the podium, Chipman said he’s learned that “there are several ways to look at this [homelessness] crisis.

“You can look at the burden it places on our health care system, our social service network, our justice system, and the sheer human impact it has on those in our emergency rooms and our first responders. You can look at it through the effect it has on our community’s sense of safety and security,” he said.

The stop in Winnipeg was the first of several in a tour Carney is taking to promote the 2026 federal budget, according to the Canadian Press.

APTN also asked SCO Grand Chief Jerry Daniels for a comment, but a spokesperson said he is not speaking to media at this time.

Emma is a Red River Métis with family roots in St. Malo, Manitoba. She graduated from RRC Polytech’s Creative Communications program in 2023 and went on to serve as a community journalist and photographer for the Free Press Community Review until she joined APTN in 2026. Equipped with a strong sense of justice, she enjoys covering stories in the central prairies for a larger audience. Her work has also appeared in Manitoba Inc. Magazine, the Free Press, and RRC Polytech’s student paper, The Projector.

“There are thousands of bylaws and codes, and other laws that First Nations have passed to govern their communities under the Indian Act that have to be addressed,” said Palmater, a lawyer and chair in Indigenous Governance at Toronto Metropolitan University. “All of these things are constitutionally protected.

content:

content:
The 2026 U.S. midterms resulted in several firsts, including the victories of Peggy Flanagan and Deb Haaland, the first Indigenous women to serve as state senator and governor, respectively, in the country’s history.




“My ancestors came to the Rio Grande Valley in the late 1200s, and this beautiful land has sustained all of us for generations,” Haaland said in her victory speech Tuesday night. “Just off this road, my grandmother was taken to boarding school, and along with my grandfather, survived through a time when the federal government attempted to strip them of their languages, traditions and identities. Yet, we are still here.”




Although the results have not been finalized, the Democrats have been favoured to win the U.S. House of Representatives (236 seats to 129) and Senate (54 to 44), a sweeping result which flipped 29 seats from red to blue, as of Wednesday afternoon.




Midterm elections are held two years after a presidential election. All members of Congress, also called the House of Representatives, are up for election, and 33 of the Senate’s 100 seats were up for grabs.




Alongside Flanagan (Minnesota) and Haaland (New Mexico), the midterms also brought in Abdul El-Sayed, the first Muslim senator in Michigan; Chris Pappas, the first openly gay senator in New Hampshire; and Keisha Lance Bottoms, the first Black female governor in Georgia.

“That didn’t happen but the actual content of the show, I was like people are going to love this, I love this, we all love this, we all love making it.”

content:
Cody Drygeese held his drum as he swore to serve the city of Yellowknife for the next four years. It was a proud moment with family in attendance, including both of his grandmothers.




The newly elected councillor is a member of the Yellowknives Dene First Nation, and is believed to be the first person from the First Nation elected to the position.




“I asked if I could swear my oath of office over my drum and they said okay,” Drygeese told 

APTN News

Drygeese received 3,439 votes in the Oct. 19 municipal election, more than any other council candidate. He was one of eight councillors sworn in alongside newly elected Mayor Melissa Syer on Nov. 2, 2026.




Drygeese said he never felt the need to put on a facade during his campaign and doesn’t plan to change who he is now that he has taken office.




“I didn’t make any false promises. I didn’t put on a politician’s face and say, vote for me,” he said. “I was just myself this entire time and I was participating in my culture and I was sharing my culture and our ceremonies with everybody.”

content:

Chief Bonnie Adolph of the Sekw’el’was (Cayoose Creek) First Nation began by outlining threats to the salmon upon which her people rely. She said that when her community wrote to the Major Projects Office asking to be consulted about listing the project under the Build Canada Act, they were told since their land was not on the proposed pipeline route, the Crown would not consult with them.

“When we told the Major Projects Office their narrow geographic approach failed to account for downstream, interconnected and cumulative environmental risks to our inherent St’át’imc title and rights,” Adolph said, “We were told that we could send comments like any member of the public, but not as a First Nation whom the Crown had a legal [duty] to consult. author: The Canadian Press
title: Difficult and unpopular decisions ahead, B.C. premier-designate Lorne Doerkson says
content:
British Columbia premier-designate Lorne Doerkson said the Conservative caucus of 63 legislators is united to lead the province but he also warned of difficult and unpopular decisions ahead.







Doerkson made the comments as newly elected Conservatives gathered for their first caucus meeting on Monday, where he told them that their job now is to govern on behalf of all constituents, no matter which party people voted for in the Oct. 24 election.




He said Conservatives owe every British Columbian the same effort and respect.




“That is the responsibility, of course, that comes from winning, but it makes making difficult decisions somewhat, maybe unpopular.”




He said that B.C. residents don’t expect perfection, but they do want honesty, effort and integrity from their government, and elected Conservatives must put the public ahead of their own party’s interests every single time.




Doerkson said people will be watching to see if his caucus will splinter as it did under the leadership of Kerry-Lynne Findlay.




“I know that there will be a lot of commentary about this caucus, and a lot of people watching to see whether or not we can hold it together,” he said.




“So, let me save everyone the suspense: this caucus is unified,” Doerkson said to cheers from the crowd.

content:

title: Family of Miranda Mamakwa seeking criminal investigation into ‘negligent’ death of mother
content:
The family of a woman who died after a federal program did not arrange transportation to medical appointments is asking for a criminal investigation.

“The criminal justice system should only be invoked where grounds exist to believe a crime has been committed,” read the statement from the family. “Public officials are as accountable as anyone else in this country for reckless acts that endanger those in their charge.”

According to her family, Miranda Mamakwa died on Sept. 8 after she didn’t receive transportation to multiple important appointments following an open-heart surgery.

She was 31 and the mother of three kids.

“Literally, the blood of Indigenous people is required for any kind of meaningful change,” said Julian Falconer, legal counsel for the family. “We have created a pattern of behavior where we only get their attention once they [Canada] have killed somebody.”

Mamakwa was a member of Fort Severn First Nation, the northernmost community in Ontario, and was relying on transportation from the Non-Insured Health Benefits Program (NIHB) to get to follow-up appointments in Thunder Bay after her surgery in April 2026.

title: ‘We take care of each other’: Voices from Montreal’s Cabot Square
content:
In Montreal’s Cabot Square, where homeless Indigenous people have gathered for decades, news that a member of the city’s police services (SPVM) had been suspended for urinating on homeless Montrealers was greeted largely without shock.




Regular visitors, as well as outreach workers from the various organizations serving unhoused populations in the west of downtown, describe relations between homeless people and police in and around Cabot Square as marked by distrust and fear.




People APTN News spoke with in Cabot Square over the last two weeks reported accumulating tickets, amounting to hundreds of dollars in fines, for fare evasion on the city’s transit system or jaywalking on Ste. Catherine Street. People who drink alcohol in the Square also said they’d received tickets for open containers. 

Few make any attempt to pay the tickets. For them, getting another ticket is simply a fact of life in Cabot Square, though one that may give police a reason to eventually arrest them.

Measuring one block by one block, Cabot Square is the only significant piece of greenspace in the western end of downtown Montreal. Located on Ste. Catherine St. at the corner of Atwater Ave., the Square is directly across from the former Montreal Forum.

title: InFocus: What’s at stake for Indigenous Peoples in the U.S. as midterm elections draw near?
content:
On Tuesday, U.S. voters will cast their ballots in the country’s midterm elections. The elections come halfway through a president’s four year term.

A record-breaking number of Indigenous candidates–at least 355–are running in this year’s race.

This week on InFocus, Pawnee/Ponca lawyer Brett Chapman tells us about the candidates he’s following and how Native Americans are feeling the impact of Trump’s second term.

A recent study by the Brookings Institution reported that the Trump administration slashed $469 million in grants and contracts to tribal communities.

“I think a big problem with the administration, the second go around, is that because of the focus by them on DEI [Diversity, Equity and Inclusion], things of that nature, they have really tried to reduce Native American issues to [being] race-based,” Chapman said.

“What defines being Native American in the United States is not being a member of a race. It’s political sovereignty in the history of over 500 tribes having treaties with the government, and they’re having their own governments. And so you’re having a government-to-government relationship.

“You’re really seeing a weakening of that when it should be stronger.”

title: Columnist says more pressing issues on agenda at First Nations meeting than abolishing Indian Act
content:
A columnist with the Hill Times says a First Nations meeting with First Ministers this week was not the appropriate venue to be discussing abolishing the more than a century-and-a-half old Indian Act.

“It seems to me that a lot of things were said at mics on that day that people really regret,” Rose LeMay said. “I don’t know anyone who would disagree that the Indian Act has to go. It’s a racist piece of segregationist law. It always has been. Whether we take out a clause here or there it’s still fundamentally a barrier to human rights. Especially for First Nations women. We’ve seen all the debate on S-2 and trying to bring in the one parent instead of the second-generation cut-off. Overall, it’s a piece of racist legislation. Was that day the day to raise it? I don’t think so.”

Lemay said it is her understanding that much more time in the meeting was spent on discussing how the government’s proposed Bill C-39 – the Building Canada Strong Act – could affect First Nations rights when it comes resource development.

title: Yukon photographer captures caribou’s extraordinary fight for survival
content:
It’s an incredible act of nature.




Two caribou. Their antlers locked in battle. One dead. The survivor, nearly immobilized by the weight of his opponent, preyed upon by a bear as foxes and birds scavenge the dead bull’s remains.




Yukon

Peter Mather

 captured the remarkable images earlier this month while filming the Southern Lakes caribou’s rut, when up to a few hundred animals gather and males spar for females.




“I have never seen anything like that before,” Mather said. “Their horns are locked together, and one of them is dead. And the bear is like sitting 10 feet away, just watching, trying to figure out what to do. It was the strangest situation.”




Mather came across the rare sighting about 20 kilometres south of Whitehorse while filming content for the Kwanlin Dün First Nation as part of a project for the Southern Lakes Caribou Steering Committee. Kwanlin Dün is one of six First Nations governments represented on the committee.




With fewer than 1,000 animals in the early 1990s, the Southern Lakes caribou, which is composed of four woodland herds, has increased to about 4,000 today, thanks in part to voluntary harvest moratoriums by First Nations.

“If you don’t take Canada’s money, the infrastructure does not get built, does not get operated, does not get maintained,” said defense lawyer Michael Rosenburg, during a hearing in the Federal Court of Appeal on Wednesday in Winnipeg. “That is the dynamic, because these First Nations have been put in this position of dependence.”

In one of the decisions, Favel said that the federal government “exerted direct control over every facet of First Nations life through legislations, regulations, policies, and practices since at least the 1880s,” and that “this extends to matters such as water infrastructure.”

title: Youths tell trial of climate change toll, from anxiety to flood and heat impacts
content:
Sadie Vipond says she was just seven years old when she began noticing the impacts of climate change.




Now a 20-year-old plaintiff in Canada’s first youth-led climate trial, Vipond described experiencing catastrophic floods in Calgary in 2013 that the city says resulted in mass evacuations, one death and $6 billion in financial losses.




“I was beginning to see different actions in my community around the climate crisis, and so I was also feeling very anxious about my future,” she told the Federal Court in Vancouver.




Vipond is one of 15 plaintiffs who are arguing that federal legislation violates their constitutional rights by continuing the trajectory of greenhouse gas emissions.




The trial that began Monday heard in an opening statement from the youths’ lawyer, Catherine Boies Parker, that the case is not about the existence of climate change but rather whether the government is “constitutionally required to stop making it worse.”




She said the Charter must protect youth from their own government’s actions.




Vipond told the court on Tuesday that she had experienced several climate change events since the floods, including wildfire smoke and intense heat.

content:
The John G. Diefenbaker Building on Sussex Drive was perhaps, in its own imperfect way, a fitting place for nearly 200 First Nations leaders, most of the country’s premiers and a prime minister to hold a meeting First Nations have wanted for more than a century.




It’s actually two buildings mashed together: a modern glass construction, like a church nave, that lets light pour in from above and gives the hallways a sense of something sacred, while behind it, the old city hall rises as a plain grey slab, a maze of stairs leading to small, dark meeting rooms. 




Outside, the chief set up teepees that strangely echo the building’s peaks.

content:

“The Government of Canada continues to fight us in Court over one of our most basic rights as human beings,” said Chief Jordna Hill of Shamattawa First Nation. “But Canada knows what it has done to First Nations people is wrong.”

“Canada ships bottled water to reserves for their federal employees, while First Nations people living under long-term drinking water advisories are forced to use the contaminated tap water.”

title: Treaty One opens campus to the first national First Nations business training centre

WTEC was founded in May 2025, but did not have a physical location until Tuesday.

“When we talk about First Nations economic development, it usually starts with what we lack,” Bluesky said at the grand opening event. “We lack capital, we lack capacity, we lack opportunities. “We bring knowledge, we bring our relationships, and we bring our determination, and we show up,” she continued. “And we’ve been providing for our people, our families, our communities, for generations, and we will continue to do so.”

She said, “aside from the paint on the walls,” the space, located on the third floor of 191 Broadway St. in downtown Winnipeg, was funded entirely by First Nations startups who have benefited from services at WTEC since its inception.

title: First Nation of Na-Cho Nyäk Dun says it’s up to citizens to decide how to move forward on Eagle mine
content:
The First Nation at the centre of the Eagle gold mine disaster in north-central Yukon says it will ultimately be up to its citizens to decide how it plans to support the sale of the mine to a foreign mining company.

The First Nation of Na-Cho Nyäk Dun, on whose traditional territory the mine is located, indicated in an Oct. 23 news release that while negotiations with Singapore-based mining and acquisitions company Boroo are in the early stages, the relationship appears positive.

“Boroo has approached our Nation with openness, respect and good faith, and we recognize the positive foundation that has been established,” it says.

“We are not turning away from mining. We believe the answer is to do it better,” it adds.

title: Carney open to conversations around ‘moving beyond’ the Indian Act
content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney says he’s open to discussions around getting rid of the Indian Act.




Passed in 1876, the controversial legislation governs people who have status under the act, reserve lands and issues related to band councils.




Carney was responding to comments made by Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew earlier in the day during the First Nations-First Ministers Meeting in Ottawa.




“Participants in the meeting raised the desirability,” Carney told reporters at the end of the meeting. “Not everybody, but other participants raised a desirability, so it’s already starting from the right place.




“And it’s not the federal government deciding something should be done.”




At the noon break, Kinew held up his First Nations status card, which he said identifies him as an “Indian within the meaning of the Indian Act.”




“It’s time to abolish the Indian Act,” Kinew said. “It’s long overdue that we have a relationship with Indigenous Peoples in Canada that reflects who we are as Canadians today.”




This isn’t the first time First Nations have called for the act to be scrapped – or a government saying it would move towards it.

title: 72 ans après sa mort, la dépouille du bébé Maxime retourne à Manawan
content:

Elle fait référence au retour de la dépouille de son oncle Maxime. Soixante-douze ans après sa mort, presqu’au jour le jour, le bébé Maxime revient enfin parmi les siens. « Bébé Maxime reviendra à Manawan, sur la terre de nos ancêtres, auprès de sa famille et de son peuple atikamekw. »

Après 43 jours à l’hôpital, bébé Maxime est mort le 5 octobre 1954.

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew says he told Prime Minister Mark Carney that Canada should abolish the Indian Act during a historic meeting with premiers and First Nations leaders.




Speaking with reporters during a midday break in the meeting Monday, Kinew held up his First Nations status card, which he said identifies him as an “Indian within the meaning of the Indian Act.”




“It’s time to abolish the Indian Act,” Kinew said. “It’s long overdue that we have a relationship with Indigenous Peoples in Canada that reflects who we are as Canadians today.”

“If they took out the occupying nation, then they could do what they wanted with the land. They could own the land,” Skip Gregg told APTN Investigates.




Gregg knows the story. It’s been passed down through the generation in Tsilhqot’in territory.




“Oral history of our people is like, yes, it was threatened to us. If you don’t give us our land or do what we want you to do, we’ll bring in smallpox,” he said.

title: Cold Lake First Nations chief acknowledges conflict as he heads to First Nations meeting in Ottawa
content:
With no Assembly of First Nations regional chief in Alberta, individual chiefs and proxies from that province will be attending Monday’s First Nations-First Ministers meeting in Ottawa.




One of those attending is Cold Lake First Nations Chief Kelsey Jacko.




“A lot of conflict has happened,” he says of discussions over who would attend. “I know AFN is going to have a lot of seats in the house. Those seats should be filled with rights holders, you know, but this is a step in the right direction,” Jacko said in an interview with 

APTN News

.




“That’s the reason why I’m going there because nobody is going to be speaking for me, for our rights or for our people.”




Jacko said he understands why Onion Lake Cree Nation and two other First Nations, Tsuut’ina and Saddle Lake Cree Nation have issued a cease and desist notice to the AFN because they speak on their own behalf.
